summary: Abraha al-Ashram, the Abyssinian viceroy of Yemen, marched on Makkah with a war elephant at the head of his army intending to destroy the Kaabah, but his campaign was miraculously obliterated by flocks of birds that rained down stones upon his troops. This event, named the Year of the Elephant, is the year in which the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ was born.
narrative:
In approximately 570 CE, Abraha ibn al-Sabbah al-Ashram — the Christian Abyssinian governor ruling Yemen on behalf of the Aksumite Empire — assembled a formidable army including at least one war elephant, named Mahmud in some accounts, and marched northward toward Makkah with the stated aim of destroying the Kaabah and redirecting the pilgrimage to a grand cathedral he had built in Sanaa called al-Qullays. The expedition was likely also motivated by political ambitions to assert Abyssinian dominance over the Arabian Peninsula trade routes.

Ibn Hisham records in his recension of Ibn Ishaq's Sirah that when Abraha's forces approached Makkah, Abd al-Muttalib ibn Hashim — the Prophet's ﷺ grandfather and the leading figure of the Quraysh — went out to meet Abraha's general. When Abd al-Muttalib's camels were seized, he came to the camp, and upon meeting Abraha he reportedly said: 'I am the lord of this House, and I have come to request the return of my camels. As for this House, it has its own Lord who will defend it.' Abd al-Muttalib then retreated and instructed the Quraysh and the Makkans to take shelter in the surrounding hills.

As Abraha's army advanced on the Kaabah, the elephant Mahmud reportedly refused to march toward Makkah — kneeling when directed toward it and rising when turned away, a detail recorded by Ibn Hisham and referenced in al-Tabari's Tarikh al-Rusul wal-Muluk. Then, as the army stood before the city, flocks of birds — described in Surah al-Fil as 'Tayr Ababeel' (birds in flocks) — appeared from the sea carrying small stones of clay (sijjil) in their beaks and claws. Each stone struck a man, passing through him and killing him. Abraha himself was afflicted, his body described as falling apart piece by piece as his army retreated toward Yemen. He died before reaching Sanaa.

Allah directly addresses this event in the Quran in Surah al-Fil (105): 'Have you not seen how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant? Did He not cause their plan to go astray? And He sent against them birds in flocks, striking them with stones of hard clay, and He made them like eaten straw.' Ibn Kathir in his Tafsir notes that the 'stones of sijjil' are pellets of baked clay or hardened mud. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir both record that some survivors of the army scattered across Arabia, dying of disease and wounds, and that the event left a profound mark on the Quraysh's sense of divine protection of the Kaabah.

Classical scholars including Ibn Hisham, al-Tabari, and Ibn Kathir are unanimous that this event occurred in the year of the Prophet's birth, making it a significant marker in Arabian chronology. The Arabs named the year 'Aam al-Fil' — the Year of the Elephant — and used it as a dating reference for generations. This miraculous preservation of the Kaabah served as a sign to the Arabs that the sacred house had a divine protector, laying spiritual groundwork for the coming of the final Prophet ﷺ within that very year.
